title: Multimodal AI Quick Revision: Vision, Diffusion and Speech
summary: Quick revision notes on vision-language models, image tokens and patches, CLIP-style contrastive training, diffusion image generation, speech-to-text and text-to-speech, and multimodal prompting. Ordered from the mental model through workflow, usage and mistakes to a cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Multimodal Models: The Mental Model
points: A vision-language model (VLM) takes image plus text in and produces text out; the image is converted into embeddings the language model reads like extra tokens
Three parts: a vision encoder (usually a ViT), a projector/connector (linear layer or MLP, sometimes cross-attention) and a language model decoder
Early fusion feeds image tokens straight into the LLM sequence (LLaVA-style); late or cross-attention fusion keeps modalities separate and attends across them (Flamingo-style)
Each modality has its own pipeline: image to patches to embeddings, audio to spectrogram to embeddings, text to subword tokens to embeddings, all landing in one shared vector space
Interview Point: What are the three components of a VLM? How does early fusion differ from cross-attention fusion? Why project vision features into the LLM embedding dimension?

chapters.title: Image Tokens, Patches and Contrastive Training
points: ViT splits an image into fixed patches (e.g. 16x16 pixels), flattens each, linearly projects it, and adds position embeddings; each patch is one image token
Token count = (H/P) x (W/P): a 224x224 image with 16x16 patches gives 14x14 = 196 tokens; doubling resolution quadruples tokens and attention cost
CLIP trains an image encoder and a text encoder jointly on image-caption pairs so matching pairs have high cosine similarity in a shared space

Contrastive loss: in a batch of N pairs, the N diagonal entries of the NxN similarity matrix are positives and the N^2-N others are negatives, with symmetric cross-entropy over rows and columns and a learned temperature
Zero-shot classification: embed prompts like 'a photo of a {class}' and pick the highest cosine similarity with the image embedding; larger batches give more negatives and better training
Interview Point: How many tokens does a 336x336 image with 14x14 patches produce? Why does CLIP need large batches? How does CLIP do zero-shot classification?

chapters.title: Diffusion Basics for Image Generation
points: Forward process gradually adds Gaussian noise to an image over T steps until it is pure noise; reverse process is a learned denoiser that removes noise step by step
Training: pick a random timestep t, add noise to a clean image, and have the network (U-Net or transformer) predict the added noise; loss is MSE between predicted and true noise
Latent diffusion (Stable Diffusion) runs diffusion in a compressed VAE latent space rather than pixel space, making it far cheaper; the VAE decoder converts the final latent to an image

Text conditioning uses a text encoder (CLIP or T5) feeding cross-attention in the denoiser; classifier-free guidance blends conditional and unconditional predictions, and higher guidance scale means closer prompt adherence but less diversity and possible oversaturation
Sampler steps trade quality for speed: fewer steps (e.g. 20-30 with DPM++ or Euler) is faster, and the seed fixes the starting noise for reproducible output
Interview Point: What does the denoiser predict during training? Why use latent space? What does the guidance scale control?

chapters.title: Speech-to-Text and Text-to-Speech
points: STT (ASR) pipeline: waveform to log-mel spectrogram to encoder-decoder transformer (e.g. Whisper) to text tokens; Whisper expects 16 kHz mono audio in 30-second windows
Word error rate (WER) = (substitutions + deletions + insertions) / reference words; lower is better, and it is the standard ASR metric
TTS pipeline: text normalization, then an acoustic model producing a mel spectrogram (or discrete audio tokens), then a vocoder (HiFi-GAN or neural codec) producing the waveform

Streaming vs batch: streaming ASR emits partial transcripts with low latency but lower accuracy; batch ASR sees full context and is more accurate; voice agents chain STT, LLM, TTS and sum their latencies
Quality is judged on naturalness (MOS score) and intelligibility; voice cloning needs consent and should be disclosed, and diarization is a separate step to label who spoke
Interview Point: What is WER and how is it computed? What does a vocoder do? Where does latency come from in a voice agent pipeline?

chapters.title: Multimodal Prompting Tips and Common Mistakes
points: Put the image before the question and refer to it explicitly ('in the chart above'); with several images, label them (Image 1, Image 2) to avoid confusion
Be specific about the task and output format: ask for JSON fields, a table, or transcribe-then-answer, rather than 'describe this'
Resolution matters: small text, thin chart lines and dense tables get lost after downscaling, so crop or tile the region of interest instead of sending the full page
Images consume many tokens and raise cost and latency; resize to the needed detail, and use OCR first for text-heavy documents when exact characters matter

Common mistakes: trusting counts, spatial relations and fine reading without verification (VLMs hallucinate), prompting with 'don't mention X' for image generation (use negative prompt instead), and ignoring audio sample rate or noise before STT
Interview Point: How do you reduce VLM hallucination on charts? When would you use OCR before a VLM? Why does image resolution affect cost?

chapters.title: Multimodal Cheat Sheet
points: Patch tokens = (H/P) x (W/P); VLM = vision encoder + projector + LLM; CLIP = contrastive loss on an NxN similarity matrix with a learned temperature
Diffusion: add noise forward, predict noise in reverse; latent diffusion uses a VAE, text enters by cross-attention, guidance scale trades diversity for prompt fit
Speech: ASR uses log-mel with encoder-decoder (Whisper, 16 kHz, 30 s windows) and WER; TTS uses acoustic model plus vocoder
Prompting: image first, label multiple images, crop for detail, request structured output, and verify counts and fine reading
Interview Point: Which single metric evaluates ASR? What are the diffusion training target and the CLIP loss? How do you cut image token cost?
